title: The Journey of a Sound
description: Follow a single chime from a vibrating bell all the way into your brain — the full path of hearing.

content.value: Hearing is a chain of steps. A source vibrates, the vibration travels through a medium as a sound wave, your ear catches it, and your brain makes sense of it. Break any link and you don't hear the sound.

🔔 source vibrates
   ↓ (sound wave travels through air)
👂 pinna collects it → ear canal → eardrum vibrates
   ↓ middle-ear bones pass it on
🧠 inner ear + auditory nerve → BRAIN recognises the sound

You have an ear on each side of your head. Because a sound reaches the nearer ear slightly sooner and louder, your brain compares the two and works out WHICH DIRECTION the sound came from. That's why you can turn straight toward someone calling your name.

People with weak hearing can use a HEARING AID — a small device that makes sounds louder before they reach the eardrum. Modern hearing aids are tiny electronic amplifiers that fit inside or behind the ear.
The ear turns air vibrations into nerve signals; the brain does the 'understanding'. Hearing is really teamwork between your ears and your brain.

Key Takeaway: Hearing is a chain — source vibrates, sound travels through a medium, the ear catches and passes on the vibration, and the brain recognises it. Two ears help us locate where a sound comes from.

quiz.question: Put the hearing steps in order: the sound wave reaches the ear AFTER…
options: the source vibrates and the wave travels through a medium
quiz.explain: First the source vibrates and the wave travels through a medium; only then does it reach the ear and finally the brain.

quiz.question: Having two ears helps us mainly to…
options: work out which direction a sound came from
quiz.explain: The brain compares the sound at each ear to locate its direction.

quiz.question: A hearing aid works by…
options: making sounds louder before they reach the eardrum
quiz.explain: A hearing aid is a small amplifier that boosts sounds for people with weak hearing.
